title: Linux Files, Permissions, and Users
subtitle: Understand Linux permissions, ownership, users, and safe access troubleshooting
intendedFor: Students who completed Linux Terminal Fundamentals and need practical, least-privilege Linux file access skills.

courseOverview.recommendedSequence: Complete Modules 1–3 with guided labs, then use one cumulative pre-seeded workspace in Module 4.
courseOverview.summary: Four-module progression from reading Linux permissions to precise chmod, identity and troubleshooting, and a secure project capstone.

moduleSummary.title: Understanding Linux Permissions
moduleSummary.coreSkill: Identify the current identity, decode mode strings, and inspect file versus directory access before changing anything.

moduleSummary.title: Managing File and Directory Access
moduleSummary.coreSkill: Change the smallest necessary permission bits on safe learner-owned fixtures; verify symbolic and octal chmod with real mode checks.

moduleSummary.title: Users, Groups, and Permission Troubleshooting
moduleSummary.coreSkill: Distinguish identity from permissions, explain privileged operations safely, investigate access errors, and understand umask.

moduleSummary.title: Capstone: Secure Project Folder
moduleSummary.coreSkill: Apply inspection, least privilege, careful mode changes, and verified parent traversal to hand off a small project.

authoringGuidance: Course 2 is an authored DRAFT; do not register it as published course or seed database records until lessons, permission-bit checker and browser end-to-end tests pass.
Prerequisite is Linux Terminal Fundamentals: pwd, ls, cd, quoted paths, safe file creation and inspection.
Use profileId bash and the existing terminal-workspace-runner; reuse shell_task terminal_workspace without a second runner or checker pipeline.
Every interactive code_input must use fixedLanguage bash, recipeType shell_task, mode terminal_workspace, and an owned fixture under /workspace.
File-tree workspaceExpectations alone do NOT validate chmod mode bits. Require an approved server-owned permission-bit verifier using stat.S_IMODE or stat -c %a, after real execution.
Never trust browser-submitted permission claims, command text alone, or a mock grader; verify against the actual sandbox workspace state.

Standard Course 2 lessons remain unprivileged. Only the three explicitly administratorLab-eligible topics may invoke scoped sudo/chown/chgrp inside a server-authorized, disposable Linux administrator sandbox; never modify host accounts, host paths, or real secrets.

Teach privilege boundaries conceptually throughout. In administratorLab-eligible topics, any hands-on privileged command must remain inside the isolated lab, subject to existing server authorization and independent trusted evidence; no privilege in ordinary lessons.
Treat chmod -R and 777 as unsafe default fixes; never teach them as problem-solving recipes.
Learner-owned fixtures must be resettable; do not chmod away the learner’s ability to clean up lab folders.
Exercise-specific workspaces should reset fixtures; cumulative module projects/capstones intentionally share a project-scoped workspace.
Check exact final permission bits for selected fixture paths and that unrelated fixture permissions remain unchanged.

Reuse the existing trusted Runner filesystem evidence and Course 1 practice-validation pipeline. The isolated seven-path capstone author QA has passed PASS-FAIL-PASS, but recorded student grading remains blocked until existing published-student authorization, compiler contracts, and attempt handling are validated.
Use safe pre-seeded run.sh content to demonstrate execution; Bash scripting instruction belongs to Course 3.
Avoid printing real secrets in prompts, sample terminal output, or screenshots; secrets.env is populated with dummy placeholder text only.
Make every sketch explain its concept, a real example, common mistake, least-privilege choice, and a task-specific Try It if technical.
Every terminal command prompt should remind students to press Enter and verify with ls -l, ls -ld or stat.
Permission-denied lessons must distinguish file bits, ownership and parent-directory traversal; avoid guessing from the error message alone.
Module 3 least-privilege decisions remain conceptual; where an administratorLab-eligible topic demonstrates sudo, execution must use the authorized disposable lab and never the Ubuntu host.
Keep exactly four modules, with meaningful lesson sections and a single capstone. Topics per module depend on concept depth; do not pad counts.
All lesson prose and keyed checks are in MODULE_1_LESSONS.md through MODULE_4_LESSONS.md and LESSON_CHECKS.json; course source is a draft until reviewed/published.

Ordinary chmod exercises require verified non-symlink, learner-owned fixtures. Only the approved capstone may require its authored root-owned README in the isolated administrator lab; verify actual modes and ownership through the existing trusted Runner before student publication.

assessmentAndDelivery.suggestedBeginnerRhythm: Two guided lessons and one sandbox lab per week, with remediation for permissions/traversal mistakes.
assessmentAndDelivery.closingNote: Learners finish able to diagnose and minimally correct common permission problems without unsafe escalation.

modules.title: Understanding Linux Permissions
modules.purpose: Identify the current identity, decode mode strings, and inspect file versus directory access before changing anything.
learningObjectives: Decode file type and owner/group/other permission triplets from ls -l.
Inspect the effective identity and group membership without hardcoded user names.
Explain why directory traversal permission can block an otherwise readable file.
guidedExercises: Inspect pre-seeded files with ls -l and directories with ls -ld.
Compare whoami, id, and groups to a file owner/group listing.
Diagnose which ancestor prevents traversal without changing fixture modes.
quizFocus: Apply user/group/other identities to access decisions.
Explain directory r/w/x and parent traversal.
modules.moduleProject: Permission Detective: explain file and parent-directory access for a pre-seeded workspace without modifying its modes.

sections.title: Reading Permissions
sections.summary: Read mode strings, owners, groups, and effective identity.

topics.title: Read Linux Permission Strings
topics.summary: Decode -rwxr-x--- and drwxr-x---: file kind and permission triplets.
learningGoals: Distinguish leading type character and owner, group, other triplets.
Translate permission bits to who may read, write, and execute.

topics.title: Inspect User Identity
topics.summary: Use whoami, id and groups to inspect the executing identity without hardcoding a username.
learningGoals: Identify who owns the current terminal session.
Explain why supplementary groups matter.

sections.title: Directory Traversal
sections.summary: Understand directory traversal and blocked ancestors.

topics.title: Files and Directories Use Bits Differently
topics.summary: Compare r/w/x for files and folders, with emphasis on directory traversal.
learningGoals: Explain directory execute as path traversal.
Understand directory write and execute are generally needed to create/remove entries.

topics.title: Diagnose Parent Directory Access
topics.summary: Use ls -ld on each parent component to find missing traversal permission.
learningGoals: Identify a blocked parent path before changing a file.
Avoid opening permissions more broadly than needed.

sections.title: Module Project
sections.summary: Read-only inspection and report of file and parent permissions.

topics.title: Project: Permission Detective
topics.summary: Inspect a supplied tree, decode modes and explain access without changing the fixtures.
learningGoals: Use ls -l, whoami, and id to produce a permission report from seeded files.

modules.title: Managing File and Directory Access
modules.purpose: Change the smallest necessary permission bits on safe learner-owned fixtures; verify symbolic and octal chmod with real mode checks.
learningObjectives: Make precise symbolic chmod changes without recursive or broad permissions.
Compute octal values for owner, group and other.
Apply safe numeric modes to files and directories and verify them using stat.
guidedExercises: Repair a supplied benign script with chmod u+x only.
Use chmod go-r to protect a test note and compare before/after.
Set a private fixture to 600 and public documentation to 644; inspect numeric modes.
quizFocus: Verify actual mode bits and least privilege.
modules.moduleProject: Secure Your Workspace: adjust only vetted learner-owned paths; check exact modes, no unrelated changes.

sections.title: Targeted Symbolic Changes
sections.summary: Use chmod u/g/o changes, script execute bits, and careful verification.

topics.title: Change Individual Bits with chmod
topics.summary: Practice chmod u+x, go-r and u=rw on learner-owned lab files.
learningGoals: Translate symbolic operators to resulting bits.
Verify change with ls -l.

topics.title: Fix Permission Denied for a Safe Script
topics.summary: Given a verified pre-seeded run.sh, use chmod u+x and safely execute it.
learningGoals: Distinguish chmod u+x from running a script.
Verify only the owner execution bit changed.

sections.title: Numeric Modes
sections.summary: Convert rwx to octal and apply exact permission modes.

topics.title: Understand Octal Permission Math
learningGoals: Convert rwx strings to three octal digits.
Calculate minimum needed bits.

topics.title: Apply and Verify Numeric Modes
topics.summary: Use chmod 600/644/700 on learner-owned lab files and verify results with stat.
learningGoals: Set chosen permissions without modifying unrelated entries.
Use stat to verify octal mode.

sections.title: Module Project
sections.summary: Secure an owned script and a private note to the specified modes.

topics.title: Project: Secure Your Workspace
topics.summary: Make and verify targeted permission changes on a trusted script and private note.
learningGoals: Fix only missing owner execution and overbroad read bits on lab-owned paths.

modules.title: Users, Groups, and Permission Troubleshooting
modules.purpose: Distinguish identity from permissions, explain privileged operations safely, investigate access errors, and understand umask.
learningObjectives: Interpret owner and group information without changing host accounts.
Explain when ownership administration would be required and why sudo is restricted.
Diagnose permission-denied failures by checking the actual access path.
Predict default mode changes under a given umask.
guidedExercises: Compare simulated owner/group listings to the current identity.
Choose safe versus privileged actions in a scenario-based quiz.
Inspect an intentionally broken learner-owned path and recommend a minimal repair.
Calculate file/directory permission results with an example umask.
quizFocus: Trace blocked parents and derive umask results.
modules.moduleProject: Shared Team Directory: analyze simulated team access, restore the minimum intended owner-owned modes, and explain privilege boundaries.

sections.title: Identity and Ownership
sections.summary: Compare owner, group, and effective identity; discuss ownership management conceptually.

topics.title: Identify Owners and Groups
topics.summary: Inspect owner/group labels and primary/supplementary group memberships.
learningGoals: Read the owner and group columns in ls -l.
Identify when a user is not the owner.

topics.title: When Ownership Must Change
topics.summary: Explain chown/chgrp use cases and privileged ownership restrictions without running either command.
learningGoals: Distinguish ownership problems from permission-bit problems.
Choose requesting administrator help rather than unsafe escalation.

sections.title: Root and Least Privilege
sections.summary: Decide when administrative access is inappropriate, without executing privileged commands.

topics.title: Why sudo Exists
topics.summary: Understand administrator privileges and why ordinary labs must not require them.
learningGoals: Choose between regular-user actions and administrative requests.

topics.title: Least Privilege in Practice
topics.summary: Evaluate commands before executing: scope, purpose, ownership, and unintended access.
learningGoals: Recognize chmod 777 and chmod -R as inappropriate beginner fixes.
Explain the smallest safe permission change.

sections.title: Troubleshooting and Defaults
sections.summary: Diagnose inaccessible paths and calculate umask outcomes.

topics.title: Trace a Permission Denied Error
topics.summary: Inspect the actual file and all parent directories before selecting a fix.
learningGoals: Read modes and ownership first.
Apply a targeted chmod only when fixture owner and intended access warrant it.

topics.title: Understand umask Safely
topics.summary: Inspect umask and understand default file/directory modes without changing global shell state.
learningGoals: Explain umask as a mask over creation permissions.
Avoid asserting a fixed umask value for every environment.

sections.title: Module Project
sections.summary: Explain and fix a controlled, learner-owned permissions mismatch.

topics.title: Project: Shared Team Directory
topics.summary: Identify a blocked path, propose least privilege, and repair only owned test fixtures.
learningGoals: Verify final modes and preserve unrelated entries.

modules.title: Capstone: Secure Project Folder
modules.purpose: Apply inspection, least privilege, careful mode changes, and verified parent traversal to hand off a small project.
learningObjectives: Secure private data, scripts, and intended shared access.
Verify actual mode bits and explain group membership assumptions.
guidedExercises: Use one cumulative /workspace/secure-project tree for all five steps in the authorized disposable administrator lab; the seven-path final state is verified from the same live workspace.
Use ls -l, ls -ld, id, and stat before chmod.
Use sudo/chown only for the explicitly authored README.md ownership requirement inside the authorized sandbox. Do not change host users/groups, external paths, or apply chmod -R or 777.
modules.moduleProject: Secure Project Folder: complete and audit five cumulative least-privilege steps.

sections.title: Final Capstone
sections.summary: Inspect, secure, verify, and document one cumulative isolated project with an intentionally root-owned README.md.

topics.title: Capstone: Secure Project Folder
topics.summary: Configure a private config, safe executable, public README, and shared directory with exact permission verification.
learningGoals: Apply least-privilege modes to the isolated capstone workspace and verify one intentionally root-owned README.md.
Verify actual mode bits, explain effective access through directories, and preserve secrets.

projectBrief.scenario: You must hand off a small development project containing a safe script, public documentation, a dummy private config, and a group-shared directory.
projectBrief.workspace: One cumulative /workspace/secure-project tree in an authorized disposable administrator sandbox, containing README.md (UID/GID 0:0), scripts/run.sh, secrets.env and shared/notes.txt (remaining entries UID/GID 1000:1000). Use only dummy credentials.
projectBrief.deliverable: A verified seven-path secure-project tree and short access explanation. The only root-owned target is README.md; never use real credentials or touch host files.
requirements: Run only in the server-authorized isolated administrator sandbox. Use the minimum sudo/chown required for README.md to be owned by 0:0; all other seven-path targets remain owned by 1000:1000. Never use recursive chmod or host paths.
Use only a safe run.sh fixture or provided script content; do not require Bash scripting knowledge beyond Course 2 before Course 3.
Check file permission bits AND parent directories; a readable file is not accessible through non-traversable parents.
Use real mode checks via an approved sandboxed verifier (stat/st_mode); workspaceExpectations alone do not check permissions.

Inspect identities with id and stat; for this explicitly authored capstone only, verify the fixed sandbox UID/GID target 1000:1000, and README.md 0:0. Do not infer host identities or group membership.
Keep stable path identities and avoid printing actual secrets or loading real environment credentials.
Use exactly one progressive capstone topic to preserve the cumulative workspace.
Never imply mode 770 guarantees access to a group unless group membership matches.

stepLadder.title: Inspect Before Changing
stepLadder.requirement: Use pwd, ls -l, ls -ld, id, and stat to inventory the supplied secure-project tree and note current modes.

stepLadder.title: Protect the Private Config
stepLadder.requirement: Set secure-project/secrets.env to 600; verify mode without displaying its contents.

stepLadder.title: Prepare the Script and Documentation
stepLadder.requirement: Set scripts/run.sh to 700 and scripts/ to 700. Keep README.md at 644 with UID/GID 0:0 using authorized scoped sudo.

stepLadder.title: Configure Team Folder Access
stepLadder.requirement: Set shared/ to 770 and shared/notes.txt to 640; keep the project root at 755, inspect UID/GID 1000:1000, and explain group membership requirements.

stepLadder.title: Verify and Document Least Privilege
stepLadder.requirement: Verify all seven authored modes and ownership values through trusted filesystem evidence, including root-owned README.md; explain why scoped sudo was necessary only for README.md and why chmod 777 was unnecessary.

notes: End-to-end author-only seven-path verifier PASS-FAIL-PASS completed; do not publish until student grading, enrollment, compiler evidence propagation, and attempt handling are validated through the established Course 1 pipeline.
Use learner-owned fixtures for ordinary chmod labs. The administratorLab-eligible capstone alone uses the approved root-owned README.md fixture inside a disposable authorized sandbox.
Privileged commands are prohibited in ordinary lessons; only administratorLab-eligible topics may demonstrate them in an authorized, disposable sandbox.
The final capstone is one progressive project with five cumulative steps.
Teach and check parent directory traversal as well as file bits.
Regular practice remains conceptual; if author-approved hands-on sudo/chown/chgrp is exposed, use only the existing administratorLab-eligible isolated runtime and server authorization.
Explain sudo conceptually in standard lessons. An approved administratorLab-eligible demonstration may test safe sudo commands in the disposable sandbox, never on a host or standard terminal.
Give a safe decision-making quiz, not executable privileged commands.
Require the existing trusted Runner to inspect seven live paths, their exact modes, and UID/GID; command-history matching and file existence alone are not grading evidence.
One cumulative five-step capstone within Module 4; do not split into additional modules.
